subject: Computer Networking
title: Email Addresses Decoded
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Email Addresses Decoded.

hook.text: user@example.com looks simple. But every part has a precise technical meaning.

buildup.text: The local part (before @) identifies the mailbox. The domain part identifies the mail server.

discovery.text: The domain maps to an MX record. The local part is matched by the receiving server to a mailbox.

twist.text: Plus addressing lets you add tags: user+shopping@example.com still reaches user. Great for filtering.

climax.text: Internationalized addresses now support non-Latin scripts. Email in Arabic or Chinese is valid.

punchline.text: The @ splits who from where. That's all email needs.

quiz.question: What does the domain part of an email address identify?
options: The mail server that handles delivery
The folder to store the email in

details.summary: An email address has two parts separated by the @ symbol: the local part identifies the user and the domain identifies the mail server. The domain is resolved through DNS to find the server.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding email address structure explains why some addresses work and others bounce. The domain part connects email to DNS, the internet's naming system.
takeaways: The local part is before the @, the domain part is after
DNS MX records map the domain to a mail server
RFC 5321 defines the rules for valid email addresses

faq.question: What characters are valid in an email address?
faq.answer: The local part can contain letters, digits, dots, hyphens, underscores, and many special characters when quoted. The domain part follows DNS rules: letters, digits, and hyphens only. Most services restrict to simple alphanumeric addresses, but the standard allows much more.

faq.question: Are email addresses case-sensitive?
faq.answer: The domain part is always case-insensitive per DNS rules. The local part is technically case-sensitive according to the RFC, but virtually all mail servers treat it as case-insensitive. Treating them as case-sensitive would cause too many delivery failures.
